fields.title: Two workloads that do not get along
fields.keyTakeaway: Transactional and analytical workloads require opposite data organization, and trying to serve both with a single storage degrades the one that matters more to the user.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Why can an analytical report take down a product even though it only reads data?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: This is the most common cause of "unexplainable" product slowdowns in companies where analytics grew faster than infrastructure. The symptom — the product lags during working hours and works great at night. A product manager who knows this pattern recognizes it from the description in a minute.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: The two types of workload are structured oppositely.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: [[oltp|OLTP]] — transactional: many short operations on individual records. Create an order, update status, read profile. Thousands per second, each touches single rows, each must be fast.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: [[olap|OLAP]] — analytical: rare heavy queries over many records. Revenue by category for the quarter broken down by stores. Dozens per hour, each reads millions of rows, each can take a minute.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *Resources.* An analytical query evicts data needed by transactions from memory. After it runs, the database works slowly for a while, even when the query has finished.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: *Locks.* Long reads hold data and hinder writes, as in the store report case discussed earlier.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: *Structure.* Transactional workloads need entire rows — the whole order at once. Analytical workloads need a single column across all rows — sums only. The exact same data organization cannot be optimal for both.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: Hence the solution everyone arrives at: **different storage systems.** Product database for OLTP, [[data-warehouse|data warehouse]] for OLAP, [[etl-elt|data pipeline]] between them.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: The problem was solved in two steps, and both were right at their time.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: First, a read-only replica — three weeks. Reports stopped interfering with orders. But the reports themselves remained slow: forty seconds, because the structure did not change, only the location did.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Then a separate storage system — six weeks. Data is transferred once an hour, structure tailored for analytics: pre-calculated aggregates by stores and days. The report opens in a second instead of forty, and this turned out to be more important than buyer speed because the partner dashboard became a sales argument.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: The intermediate step with the replica was not redundant: it stopped losses in three weeks instead of six.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Separation costs money and introduces delay. A small product does not need it: up to a certain volume, analytics on the product database at night work perfectly. The sign that it is time is when analytical queries start happening during working hours and become regular.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Transactional and analytical workloads require opposite data organization, and trying to serve both with a single storage degrades the one that matters more to the user.
